name: Neuroscience Free Will

nodeContents.response:
**No — and the strongest arguments against it are empirical, not philosophical.**

Sorting the field the way you asked:

### Claims that actually rest on data (and have moved)

- **"The readiness potential is the brain's early decision."** This was the load-bearing empirical premise, and it has largely collapsed. ([What Is the Readiness Potential?: Trends in Cognitive Sciences](https://www.cell.com/trends/cognitive-sciences/fulltext/S1364-6613%2821%2900093-0)) The RP is generated by sampling only epochs that culminate in movement — we never see what happens when no movement is triggered — raising the possibility that it's an artifact of biased sampling. ([An accumulator model for spontaneous neural activity prior to self-initiated movement | PNAS](https://www.pnas.org/doi/10.1073/pnas.1210467109)) A decision threshold applied to autocorrelated noise reproduces both the RP's shape and the distribution of waiting times in Libet's task. On that reading the RP isn't a decision already made; ([Confusions regarding stochastic fluctuations and accumulators in spontaneous movements | bioRxiv](https://www.biorxiv.org/content/10.1101/2021.06.04.447111v3.full)) the decision happens *late*, at threshold crossing, close to the reported time of deciding.
- **Scope.** ([Neural precursors of decisions that matter—an ERP study of deliberate and arbitrary choice](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC6809608/)) In a \$1000 charitable-donation task, RPs appeared for arbitrary choices but were strikingly absent for deliberate ones — consistent with the RP tracking random fluctuations that drive coin-flip choices only. Whatever Libet found, it may not generalize to the choices anyone cares about.
- **Predictive strength.** The famous fMRI decoding results run at roughly 60% on binary choices seconds ahead — a detectable bias, not a determination.

### Philosophy wearing a lab coat

- The inference from "unconscious neural precursor" to "*you* didn't decide" presupposes that the self is only the conscious part. That's a premise smuggled in, not measured.
- Determinism is not an experimental finding. If universal physical determination threatens free will, milliseconds add nothing; if it doesn't, they still add nothing.
- Treating a decision as a dated point-event with a timestamp is a metaphysical commitment built into the experimental design.

Tellingly, Libet himself allowed that actions arising from longer-timescale conscious deliberation escape these timing problems, and philosophers have noted that few responsibility-relevant decisions fit the Libet profile at all.

Two directions from here: what the RP *is* now taken to be, or what an experiment would have to show to bear on free will at all.

nodeContents.query: Does quantum randomness rescue free will?
nodeContents.response:
**No — and it fails at the philosophy before the physics ever gets a vote.**

### The part that needs no lab

The luck objection is a priori: if my choice traces to an undetermined event, then holding my reasons, character and history fixed, the other option could have occurred. That's not more control, it's less. Randomness converts a determined outcome into an unowned one — a worse position for responsibility, not a better one. No experiment bears on this.

The one non-trivial rejoinder is Balaguer's, and it's worth knowing precisely because it does cash out empirically. He restricts the claim to *torn decisions* — options tied for best, where you consciously pick without a reason that settles it. ([Frontiers | Free Will, Determinism, and Epiphenomenalism](https://www.frontiersin.org/journals/psychology/articles/10.3389/fpsyg.2018.02623/full)) His "central libertarian thesis" inverts the randomness argument: the right kind of indeterminacy implies non-randomness rather than randomness, because ([Determinism and Its Relevance to the Free-Will Question 15 Mark Balaguer](https://www.calstatela.edu/sites/default/files/determinism_and_its_relevance_to_the_free-will_question.pdf)) if the decision is undetermined at the moment of choice, nothing outside the agent's conscious reasons comes in and fixes which option wins. On that view, whether libertarianism is true reduces to the empirical question of whether such decisions are genuinely undetermined. Critics (Kane included) press that this still looks like luck deciding between tied options.

### The part that needs a lab, and loses ([Importance of quantum decoherence in brain processes - ADS](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2000PhRvE..61.4194T/abstract))

Tegmark's estimates put neural decoherence timescales at ~$10^{-13}$–$10^{-20}$ s against dynamical timescales of ~$10^{-3}$–$10^{-1}$ s — ten-plus orders of magnitude. ([Quantum computation in brain microtubules: Decoherence and biological feasibility | Phys. Rev. E](https://link.aps.org/doi/10.1103/PhysRevE.65.061901)) Hameroff and colleagues contest the setup and recover longer times, but nothing there is established. And note the asymmetry: the amplification story only has to fail once, whereas free will would need quantum noise steered *toward* the agent's reasons — a mechanism nobody has proposed.

A footnote people misread: Conway–Kochen's "free will theorem" is a conditional — *if* experimenters are free, particles are unpredictable too — not a rescue.

The live question this leaves open is what neural determinism at decision points would actually have to look like to be settled either way, which is a different experiment from the ones in [[e64201c4-5f84-484d-a7b8-cfb0be3216aa]].

brief: Headlines keep claiming the brain “decides before you do.” I want to know whether the neuroscience actually shows that, and whether it would matter for free will if it did. I studied a little philosophy of mind years ago — skip the intro-course taxonomy of positions. What I care about: which arguments actually depend on experimental results, and which are philosophy wearing a lab coat.

suggestions.text: What experiment could distinguish a genuinely settled decision from mere neural bias or preparation before action?
How robust is the finding that readiness potentials disappear for deliberate, consequential choices, and what are its main methodological weaknesses?
What does roughly 60% advance prediction actually show once temporal leakage, choice-history effects, and out-of-sample replication are accounted for?
